title: The Question of a Wife
body: The cold-weather mail brings your sister's letter from Surrey, smelling faintly of damp wool and the old anxieties. She is glad the posting is a good one. She wonders, in the gentlest hand, whether you do not find it lonely; whether a man in your position ought not, by now, to have someone; whether — she names a Miss Carteret, lately gone out to Bombay to an uncle — you might not, when you are next down that way … Nowhere does she write that you are eight-and-twenty and still a bachelor. Every line says it.

choices.label: Write back that the district is wife enough for a while yet.
choices.outcome: You put together a light, deflecting paragraph on the weight of the work and the smallness of the station, and post it by the cold-weather dak. True enough, so far as it goes. Of the long evenings you say nothing, to her or to yourself.

choices.label: Confess, on paper, that you have lately thought about it.
choices.outcome: You admit more than you meant to — that the bungalow is very large at night, that a man cannot dine with the district for ever — and feel, sealing it, both lighter and faintly exposed. Your sister will read it three times, and begin at once to make arrangements you have not sanctioned.

choices.label: Reply about the shooting and the crops, and answer nothing.
choices.outcome: Two dutiful pages on the partridge-shooting and the state of the winter rice, and not one word on the matter she raised. She has a brother; she will understand, and she will not be put off.

title: The Marriage Question
body: The hot weather brings it to a head, as it brings everything. Miss Carteret, it appears, is up in the same hills as half the marriageable English in the province — the ‘fishing fleet,’ the Club calls them, not always unkindly. There is also, the city being what it is, a quieter arrangement a lonely man may make and no one speak of. And there is the third road, the one the Service half-expects of its best men: no wife at all, and the district for a bride. The lamp hisses. The long evening waits on your answer.

choices.label: Go up on leave, court Miss Carteret, and marry.
choices.outcome: You take your leave, and your courage, up the hill, and come down in six weeks an engaged man and presently a married one. It is sudden, and it frightens you rather more than the district does. The bungalow acquires curtains, a piano no one plays well, and a reason to come home before dark.

choices.label: Keep a quiet house in the city, and tell no one.
choices.outcome: There is a girl, and a small shuttered house down a lane the sahibs do not walk, with pigeons on the coping and cool water in the chatties. The arrangement is as old as the country and as unmentionable at the Club. It keeps a man human; on a bad day it could keep him from a knighthood. You decide the warmth is worth it.

choices.label: Marry the Service; a District Officer has no business with a wife.
choices.outcome: You let the season pass, and Miss Carteret with it, and give the district what another man would give a household. Simla approves of the unencumbered officer. At two in the morning, in a bungalow the size of a barn, the unencumbered officer is less sure. The evenings will send in their bill.

title: The Mail That Has Never Missed
body: Five years, and her letter has never once missed the monthly boat: Kotra, the paper-chase, the leave you asked and got, and everything since, kept alive in ink across eleven thousand miles. This one is different. Her uncle the judge has retired at last; the Surrey house is to be given up; and — set down lightly, the way she rides — ‘I am asked at every dinner now whether I am engaged. I laughed it off again on Tuesday. The laugh is wearing thin.’ She does not press. She has never pressed; that is rather the point of her. The letter lies on the desk like a settlement notice.

choices.label: Answer the whole of it, honestly, the day it arrives.
choices.outcome: You write past midnight and say what five years of careful mail has walked around: that the district is a posting, but she has been the career. It goes down to the boat with the official bag, and you sleep better than you have since the Gazette. What she does with it is now the only file in India you cannot call for.

choices.label: Reply warmly, and step around the question one mail more.
choices.outcome: Four affectionate, well-made pages about the settlement and the new bund, and not one word on the only matter the letter raised. You are eight-and-twenty and a Collector, and you have answered a direct question with a district report. She will read it twice, put it in the sandalwood box with the others, and begin — very quietly — to count.

choices.label: Set it in the drawer until the season's work eases.
choices.outcome: The season's work does not ease; season's work never does. The letter waits under the crop forecast with its question standing, and for the first time in five years the boat goes without your answer aboard. In Surrey, a fortnight hence, the silence will be understood.

title: Five Years Is an Answer Too
body: The hot weather brings it to a head, as it brings everything. Her letter this month is the shortest she has ever sent: the house is given up at Michaelmas; an aunt in Cheltenham offers a room; and a Major Enderby, home from Peshawar, has taken to calling on Thursdays — set down without comment, as she would report a change in the weather. The code is not hard. She has waited from three-and-twenty to eight-and-twenty on a probationer’s half-promise, the fishing fleet sails both ways, and a man who will not decide is deciding. The pen is in your hand. The mail goes down Tuesday.

choices.label: Write for her at last: come out in October, and marry.
choices.outcome: Eleven words of wire, and five years behind each of them. Her answer comes back by the same boat — she had, it turns out, already spoken to the P&O agent — and in October the girl from the Christmas camp comes down the gangway at Bombay and looks at you as she looked back from the tonga at Kotra. The bungalow acquires curtains, a seat on a horse that shames the district, and a reason to come home before dark. Major Enderby, you learn long afterwards, never stood a chance and knew it.

choices.label: Ask her to wait one year more; a first district is no place for a bride.
choices.outcome: Prudent, provident, and every word of it true: the famine ledger, the fever season, the bungalow half a day from a doctor. You post it believing it, and for a week feel responsible and just. Her reply is two pages of perfect kindness with something gone out of them — the thing that made five years of mail feel like a held hand. She does not write, and neither do you, that you have asked a woman of eight-and-twenty to bet one more year on a man who has twice been dealt his cards and folded them.

choices.label: Release her; five years is enough to ask of anyone.
choices.outcome: You write the generous letter, the one that sets her free with every grace, and it takes three drafts because your hand will not stay level. It is the finest thing you have ever done on paper, and the dearest. Her answer is one page: she thanks you for a candour she had, she says, stopped expecting, and wishes you what you wish yourself — a line you will read many times over the years, in the long evenings, without ever deciding how much mercy was in it.

title: Beyond the Pale
body: The arrangement has become, without either of you deciding it, something nearer a marriage. She keeps the little house as a memsahib keeps a bungalow; there is always cool water in the chatties, and a rose in a brass pot by the window; and she has taught you the vernacular past the point of use and into the point of tenderness. Now the station has begun, as stations do, to half-notice a light in a lane where a sahib’s light has no business. To end it would take one evening and no witnesses. To keep it will cost something not yet priced.

choices.label: Keep it, discreetly, and let the station think what it likes.
choices.outcome: You keep faith with the one person in the district who wants nothing of the Collector and everything of the man. It costs you, in the currency of the billiard-room, more than you will ever quite total. You find, somewhat to your surprise, that you would pay it again.

choices.label: Keep it, but at arm’s length — the career comes first.
choices.outcome: You draw the line the Service would draw: the house kept, the heart withdrawn, the visits fewer, the door of yourself shut. She understands before you speak — her people have watched sahibs come to this for a hundred years. ‘As the Presence wishes,’ she says, and asks for nothing, which is worse than any reproach.

choices.label: End it now, cleanly, before it is discovered.
choices.outcome: It is done prudently: a settlement, a closed door, a lane you will not ride down again. Your career is safe; your conscience is not. Riding home in the dark, you understand what sort of man the Service has been quietly making of you all along.

title: The Long Evenings
body: The rains shut you in, and the bungalow you chose over a wife is very large in the dark. There is the district by day, which is a mercy, and the evening, which is not: the punkah, the rain on the thatch, the bottle, and eleven hundred miles between you and anyone who knew you before India. Other men have gone quietly to pieces in this very chair. You watched them do it. You had thought yourself better made.

choices.label: Beat it with iron routine — work, the dawn ride, no drink after nine.
choices.outcome: You govern yourself as you govern the district: by the timetable and the shut door. It is joyless, and it holds. The Service buries a few of its bachelors every hot weather; you will not be one of them this year, and you try not to notice how narrow it ran.

choices.label: Pour it all into the district; be married to the work in earnest.
choices.outcome: You give the year what a wife might have had, and the district takes all of it. The returns are the best in the Division, and you are the emptiest man at the Club. Simla will read the figures and mark you for advancement. Nobody reads the evenings.

choices.label: Let the evenings win, a little, most nights.
choices.outcome: Not disgrace — nothing so definite — only a softening, a later start, a decanter lower each morning than a prudent man’s. The district notices before you do. It files the sahib who drinks alone under a heading that holds a sorrowful lot of names.
